<problem>
For a finite group \(G\), let \(|G|\) denote its order and let \(k(G)\) denote its number of conjugacy classes. Define
\[
\mathcal E=\left\{p>451:\ p\text{ is prime and there exists a finite solvable group }G\text{ such that }p^2\mid |G|\text{ and }k(G)<\frac{49p+451}{60}\right\}.
\]
Determine \(\mathcal E\) exactly as an explicit set of primes.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must give an explicit set of primes equal to \(\mathcal E\), and establish that every listed prime admits such a finite solvable group and that no other prime greater than 451 does.

One agent, working alone, was asked to find the answer, which it was not told, and to prove it, writing Python that checks every step. Its run ended: all agents idle, the judge found the proof complete. Read from its record, the answer it ended with is \(\mathcal E=\{631,991,1063,1279,1423,2143,2287,2503,2719\}\).. 7	The strict inequality in the question matters. In particular, a family associated with the integer \(10\) must be excluded without replacing \(<\) by \(\leq\).
8	
9	I give the group-theoretic reduction, the remaining arithmetic, and executable verification code. The code constructs witnesses as matrix groups; it does not merely print the proposed answer.
10	
11	## 1. Classical structural facts used
12	
13	I use the following classical finite-group results.
14	
15	1. **Frattini facts for solvable groups.**
16	   * If \(X\) is solvable and \(X/\Phi(X)\) has cyclic Sylow \(p\)-subgroups, then \(X\) has cyclic Sylow \(p\)-subgroups.
17	   * If \(X\) is solvable and \(\Phi(X)=1\), then \(F(X)\) is the direct product of the minimal normal subgroups of \(X\), and \(F(X)\) has a complement.
18	
19	   These are standard consequences of the Gaschütz theory of Frattini extensions and complements. The first statement here is specifically about **cyclic Sylow subgroups**; no general assertion that \(\Phi(X)\cap P\leq\Phi(P)\) is being used.
20	
21	2. **The primitive solvable linear-group structure theorem.**  
22	   Suppose that \(K\leq\mathrm{GL}_d(p)\) is solvable, irreducible and linearly primitive. There are a cyclic normal subgroup \(U\), positive integers \(e,f\) with \(ef\leq d\), and
23	   \[
24	   e=\prod_r r^{a_r},
25	   \qquad
26	   C(e)=e^2\prod_r|\mathrm{Sp}_{2a_r}(r)|,
27	   \tag{1}
28	   \]
29	   such that
30	   \[
31	   |U|\mid p^f-1,\qquad
32	   |K:U|\leq fC(e),\qquad
33	   |K:C_K(U)|\leq f.
34	   \tag{2}
35	   \]
36	   Empty products have value \(1\).
37	
38	   This is the usual Fitting/symplectic structure theorem for solvable primitive linear groups: the noncyclic part of the Fitting subgroup is a central product of extraspecial groups, its quotient by the cyclic part has order \(e^2\), and its outer action embeds in the indicated symplectic groups. The field action has order at most \(f\). Only the consequences (1)–(2) are needed below.
39	
40	3. A finite subgroup of \(\mathrm{PGL}_2\) of order prime to the characteristic is cyclic, dihedral, \(A_4,S_4\), or \(A_5\). In the solvable case \(A_5\) is absent.
41	
42	These are classical structural results, not the recent bound asked about in the question.
43	
44	Write
45	\[
46	T(p)=\frac{49p+451}{60}.
47	\]
48	For \(p>451\), we have \(T(p)<p\).
49	
50	## 2. Reduction to an irreducible affine group
51	
52	Fix \(p>451\), and suppose a solvable group satisfying the question exists. Choose one, \(G\), of minimum order.
53	
54	First, its Sylow \(p\)-subgroups cannot be cyclic. Indeed, if \(P\) is cyclic and \(p^2\mid |P|\), fusion in \(P\) is controlled by \(N_G(P)\). The induced automorphism group is a \(p'\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(P)\), so has order at most \(p-1\). The \(p(p-1)\) elements of order \(p^2\) therefore give at least \(p\) conjugacy classes. Together with the identity,
55	\[
56	k(G)\geq p+1>T(p).
57	\tag{3}
58	\]
59	
60	If \(\Phi(G)\ne1\) and \(p^2\mid |G/\Phi(G)|\), minimality, together with \(k(G)\geq k(G/\Phi(G))\), is a contradiction. Otherwise \(G/\Phi(G)\) has cyclic Sylow \(p\)-subgroups, so the first Frattini fact and (3) again give a contradiction. Thus
61	\[
62	\Phi(G)=1.
63	\]
64	
65	Every minimal normal subgroup of \(G\) is a \(p\)-group: quotienting by a minimal normal \(q\)-subgroup with \(q\ne p\) would contradict minimality.
66	
67	Consequently,
68	\[
69	G=V\rtimes H,\qquad V=F(G),
70	\]
71	where \(V\) is elementary abelian of \(p\)-power order and \(H\) acts faithfully and completely reducibly.
72	
73	If \(G\) has two distinct minimal normal subgroups \(N_1,N_2\), write \(|G|_p=p^b\). Minimality gives
74	\[
75	|N_i|\geq p^{b-1}.
76	\]
77	Since \(N_1\cap N_2=1\), we obtain \(2(b-1)\leq b\), hence \(b=2\). Thus \(V\cong C_p^2\), its two constituents have dimension one, and \(H\) is abelian. In that case
78	\[
79	k(G)\geq |H|+\frac{p^2-1}{|H|}
80	\geq 2\sqrt{p^2-1}>p,
81	\]
82	another contradiction.
83	
84	We have proved that
85	\[
86	G=V\rtimes H,\qquad V\cong\mathbb F_p^n,\quad n\geq2,
87	\tag{4}
88	\]
89	with \(H\) solvable and irreducible.
90	
91	We will repeatedly use the elementary affine lower bound
92	\[
93	k(V\rtimes H)\geq k(H)+\frac{|V|-1}{|H|}.
94	\tag{5}
95	\]
96	For example, this follows from the little-groups formula on the characters of the abelian normal subgroup \(V\): each nonzero orbit contributes at least one class.
97	
98	## 3. Only dimension two, with projective image \(S_4\), can occur
99	
100	Here are the estimates that make this reduction uniform in the dimension.
101	
102	### 3.1 Primitive linear groups
103	
104	For \(C(e)\) in (1),
105	\[
106	C(1)=1,\qquad C(2)=24,\qquad C(3)=216,
107	\]
108	and
109	\[
110	C(e)\leq e^{\,2\log_2e+3}.
111	\tag{6}
112	\]
113	Indeed,
114	\[
115	|\mathrm{Sp}_{2a}(r)|<r^{2a^2+a},
116	\]
117	and \(a\leq\log_2e\).
118	
119	For \(e\geq4\),
120	\[
121	e^{\,2\log_2e+3}<4\cdot451^{e-2}.
122	\tag{7}
123	\]
124	One way to check this for all real \(e\geq4\) is to take logarithms. The difference is positive at \(e=4\), and its derivative is
125	\[
126	\log451-\frac{4\log e/\log2+3}{e}>0.
127	\]
128	The fraction on the right is decreasing for \(e\geq4\).
129	
130	Together with the displayed values of \(C(1),C(2),C(3)\), (7), and induction on \(f\), this gives
131	\[
132	f^2C(e)\leq4p^{d-2}\quad(d\geq3),
133	\tag{8}
134	\]
135	whenever \(ef\leq d\) and \(p>451\). For completeness, the small starting cases in this induction are
136	\[
137	216<4\cdot451,\qquad
138	4^7<4\cdot451^2,\qquad
139	4\cdot24<4\cdot451^2,\qquad
140	9<4\cdot451.
141	\]
142	For dimension two the corresponding bound is \(f^2C(e)\leq24\), and for dimension one it is \(1\).
143	
144	If \(H\) is linearly primitive, (2) gives \(k(H)\geq |U|/f\). Consequently (5) and AM–GM give
145	\[
146	k(V\rtimes H)
147	\geq 2\sqrt{\frac{p^n-1}{f^2C(e)}}.
148	\tag{9}
149	\]
150	For \(n\geq3\), (8) makes the right-hand side larger than \(p-1\). Since the left-hand side is integral,
151	\[
152	k(V\rtimes H)\geq p.
153	\tag{10}
154	\]
155	
156	### 3.2 Imprimitive linear groups
157	
158	We also need to exclude linearly imprimitive \(H\).
159	
160	A solvable permutation group of degree \(t\) has order at most \(4^{t-1}\). This follows by induction on block systems: a primitive solvable group has affine degree \(r^a\) and order at most
161	\[
162	r^{a^2+a}\leq4^{r^a-1}.
163	\]
164	The last inequality follows from \(a(a+1)\leq2(2^a-1)\), and monotonicity in \(r\geq2\).
165	
166	Choose a system of \(t\geq2\) blocks of minimum block dimension \(d\), so \(n=dt\). The induced group \(K\) on a block is irreducible and primitive, and
167	\[
168	H\leq K\wr T
169	\]
170	for a solvable permutation group \(T\) of degree \(t\).
171	
172	Apply (1)–(2) to \(K\), and put \(D=H\cap U^t\). Then
173	\[
174	|H:D|\leq(fC(e))^t|T|,
175	\qquad
176	|H:C_H(D)|\leq f^t|T|.
177	\]
178	Thus
179	\[
180	k(V\rtimes H)\geq
181	2\sqrt{\frac{p^{dt}-1}{(f^2C(e))^t|T|^2}}.
182	\tag{11}
183	\]
184	
185	In every case the denominator in (11) is at most \(4p^{dt-2}\):
186	
187	* If \(d=1,t=2\), use \(|T|\leq2\).
188	* If \(d=1,t\geq3\), use
189	  \[
190	  16^{t-1}\leq4p^{t-2}.
191	  \]
192	* If \(d=2\), use
193	  \[
194	  24^t16^{t-1}<4p^{2t-2}.
195	  \]
196	* If \(d\geq3\), use (8) and
197	  \[
198	  4^{t-1}16^{t-1}=64^{t-1}<p^{2t-2}.
199	  \]
200	
201	The first terms of the two geometric inequalities are respectively
202	\(256<4\cdot451\) and \(24^2\cdot16<4\cdot451^2\); their subsequent ratios also satisfy the required inequalities.
203	
204	Again (11) is larger than \(p-1\), so (10) holds.
205	
206	Therefore our counterexample must have \(n=2\), and \(H\) is linearly primitive.
207	
208	### 3.3 Projective image in dimension two
209	
210	The primitive structure theorem in dimension two shows that \(p\nmid |H|\): here the only possible factors outside \(U\) divide \(24\), while \(|U|\mid p^f-1\) with \(f\leq2\).
211	
212	Let \(Z=H\cap\mathbb F_p^\times I\), and put \(m=|Z|\). The projective image is cyclic, dihedral, \(A_4\), or \(S_4\).
213	
214	If it is cyclic or dihedral, \(H\) has an abelian subgroup of index at most two. Hence \(k(H)\geq |H|/4\), and
215	\[
216	k(G)\geq\frac{|H|}{4}+\frac{p^2-1}{|H|}
217	\geq\sqrt{p^2-1}>p-1.
218	\]
219	This excludes those cases.
220	
221	For projective image \(A_4\) or \(S_4\), \(m\) is even. In fact, lifts of the projective four-group contain \(Q_8\), including \(-I\).
222	
223	Counting classes above the projective classes gives
224	\[
225	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
226	H/Z&|H|&k(H)\\ \hline
227	A_4&12m&7m/2\\
228	S_4&24m&4m.
229	\end{array}
230	\tag{12}
231	\]
232	Here is the class-count calculation. The identity projective class contributes \(m\) classes. Each projective involution class contributes \(m/2\) classes: the centralizer of a lift has projective index two in the projective centralizer, since distinct commuting projective involutions have anticommuting lifts. Each projective class of order three or four contributes \(m\) classes. There is one involution class and two order-three classes in \(A_4\), and two involution classes, one order-three class and one order-four class in \(S_4\).
233	
234	For \(A_4\), (5) and (12) give
235	\[
236	k(G)\geq\frac{7m}{2}+\frac{p^2-1}{12m}
237	\geq2\sqrt{\frac{7(p^2-1)}{24}}>p.
238	\]
239	
240	We have therefore proved the crucial reduction:
241	\[
242	\boxed{
243	G=\mathbb F_p^2\rtimes H,\quad
244	H/Z\cong S_4,\quad
245	m=|Z|\text{ even},\quad
246	|H|=24m,\quad k(H)=4m.
247	}
248	\tag{13}
249	\]
250	
251	## 4. The extra contribution from fixed vectors
252	
253	We need more than (5) in a few cases.
254	
255	For a \(p'\)-subgroup \(H\leq\mathrm{GL}_2(p)\), each nonzero-vector stabilizer \(H_v\) is cyclic. Indeed, its action on \(V/\langle v\rangle\) is faithful, since the kernel would be a unipotent \(p\)-group.
256	
257	The coprime affine class formula consequently gives
258	\[
259	k(V\rtimes H)
260	=
261	k(H)+\frac{p^2-1}{|H|}
262	+\frac1{|H|}
263	\sum_{v\ne0}\bigl(|H_v|^2-1\bigr).
264	\tag{14}
265	\]
266	One can obtain this from the little-groups formula on the dual of \(V\). The vector and dual actions have the same numbers of fixed points for every subgroup of \(H\), by complete reducibility, and hence the same stabilizer-orbit counts.
267	
268	Thus, if at least six projective lines have stabilizers of order at least two,
269	\[
270	k(G)\geq4m+\frac{p^2-1}{24m}+\frac{3(p-1)}{4m}.
271	\tag{15}
272	\]
273	If at least eight lines have stabilizers of order at least three, the last contribution is instead at least
274	\[
275	\frac{8(p-1)}{3m}.
276	\tag{16}
277	\]
278	
279	Put
280	\[
281	d=\frac{p-1}{m},\qquad
282	B_d(p)=\frac{4(p-1)}d+\frac{d(p+1)}{24}.
283	\tag{17}
284	\]
285	By (13)–(14),
286	\[
287	k(G)\geq B_d(p).
288	\tag{18}
289	\]
290	
291	## 5. Restricting the integer \(d\)
292	
293	Straight calculation gives
294	\[
295	\begin{array}{c|c}
296	d&T(p)-B_d(p)\\ \hline
297	7&(2183-13p)/280\\
298	8&(461-p)/60\\
299	9&(2731-p)/360\\
300	10&15/2\\
301	11&(9797-7p)/1320\\
302	12&(441-p)/60.
303	\end{array}
304	\tag{19}
305	\]
306	
307	For \(p>451\), \(B_d(p)\) decreases for \(1\leq d\leq9\) and increases for \(d\geq10\). The rows \(d=7,12\) therefore exclude all \(d\leq7\) and \(d\geq12\).
308	
309	For \(d=8\), (19) requires \(451<p<461\), so \(p=457\); but then \(m=(p-1)/8=57\) is odd, contrary to (13).
310	
311	Only \(d=9,10,11\) remain.
312	
313	### 5.1 Excluding \(d=10\)
314	
315	Since \(m=(p-1)/10\) is even, \(p\equiv1\pmod{20}\), so \(p\equiv1\) or \(5\pmod8\).
316	
317	If \(p\equiv1\pmod8\), then \(4\mid m\). The subgroup \(Q_8\leq H\) has three noncentral projective involutions. Their six eigenlines are distinct; since their eigenvalues are fourth roots of unity, they lie in the scalar subgroup of order \(m\). Each of these six lines consequently has nontrivial point stabilizer. From (15),
318	\[
319	k(G)\geq B_{10}(p)+\frac{3\cdot10}{4}=T(p),
320	\]
321	which excludes the strict inequality.
322	
323	If \(p\equiv5\pmod8\), such an \(H\) cannot have scalar index \(10\). To see this, choose \(h\in H\) whose projective image has order four. It has eigenvalues \(\lambda,i\lambda\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), where \(i^2=-1\). Its square has the same projective image as a suitable \(q\in Q_8\), whose eigenvalues are \(i,-i\). Therefore \(h^2q^{-1}=sI\) with
324	\[
325	s=\pm i\lambda^2.
326	\]
327	Because \(p\equiv5\pmod8\), this scalar is a nonsquare. But \(sI\in Z\), whereas \(Z\), having even index \(10\) in \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), consists entirely of squares. This is impossible.
328	
329	Thus \(d=10\) gives no member of \(\mathcal E\).
330	
331	### 5.2 The odd indices \(d=9,11\)
332	
333	For these indices,
334	\[
335	T(p)-B_d(p)<\frac{3d}{4}\qquad(p>451).
336	\tag{20}
337	\]
338	
339	If a projective involution is split, its eigenvalues, after choosing a lift, have squares in the scalar group \(Z\). Since \(d\) is odd, its eigenvalues themselves lie in \(Z\). Thus its two eigenlines have nontrivial point stabilizer.
340	
341	We recall the elementary splitting facts for projective \(S_4\):
342	
343	* If \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), the three double transpositions are split.
344	* If \(p\equiv3\pmod8\), the six transpositions are split.
345	* If \(p\equiv7\pmod8\), the projective \(S_4\) is contained in \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(p)\).
346	
347	For clarity, these follow from the determinant character to
348	\(\mathbb F_p^\times/(\mathbb F_p^\times)^2\). A projective involution is split precisely when minus its determinant is a square. Double transpositions lie in the kernel. Examining an order-four element in the split or nonsplit torus shows that the determinant character on \(S_4\) is nontrivial for \(p\equiv3,5\pmod8\), and trivial for \(p\equiv1,7\pmod8\).
349	
350	In either of the first two cases there are at least six distinct split involution eigenlines. Equations (15) and (20) exclude the strict inequality. Hence necessarily
351	\[
352	p\equiv7\pmod8.
353	\tag{21}
354	\]
355	
356	Let \(O\cong2.S_4\) be the inverse image of this projective \(S_4\) in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(p)\), the binary octahedral group. Because \(d\) is odd,
357	\[
358	H=ZO.
359	\tag{22}
360	\]
361	Indeed, any possible scalar twist would give a homomorphism from \(O\), whose abelianization has order two, to a cyclic group of odd order \(d\), and is therefore trivial.
362	
363	If \(3\mid m\), the order-three projective elements give eight distinct eigenlines whose point stabilizers have order at least three. Equation (16) contributes \(8d/3\), more than the allowance in (20). Therefore
364	\[
365	3\nmid m.
366	\tag{23}
367	\]
368	
369	Conversely, under (21)–(23), \(H=ZO\) is fixed-point-free on the nonzero vectors. The noncentral elements of \(O\) have eigenvalues of orders \(3,4,6\), or \(8\). But \(m\) has 2-part exactly \(2\), and \(3\nmid m\), so none of these eigenvalues belongs to \(Z\). Thus
370	\[
371	k(\mathbb F_p^2\rtimes H)=B_d(p).
372	\tag{24}
373	\]
374	
375	We have reduced the entire problem to the following two finite searches:
376	\[
377	\begin{array}{ll}
378	d=9:&451<p<2731,\quad p\equiv7\pmod8,\quad
379	18\mid p-1,\quad 3\nmid (p-1)/9;\\[2mm]
380	d=11:&451<p<9797/7,\quad p\equiv7\pmod8,\quad
381	22\mid p-1,\quad 3\nmid (p-1)/11.
382	\end{array}
383	\tag{25}
384	\]
385	Here \(p\) must be prime.
386	
387	The first line gives exactly the nine primes in the answer. The second gives none.
388	
389	## 6. Explicit witnesses and executable verification
390	
391	For each of the nine primes, take
392	\[
393	m=(p-1)/9,\qquad H=\langle Z,O\rangle,\qquad
394	G=\mathbb F_p^2\rtimes H.
395	\]
396	Then \(H\) is solvable: \(O\) has normal subgroup \(Q_8\), with quotient of order six, and adjoining scalar matrices is a central extension. Also,
397	\[
398	|H|=24m,\qquad k(H)=4m,
399	\]
400	and \(H\) is fixed-point-free on nonzero vectors. Therefore
401	\[
402	k(G)=4m+\frac{p^2-1}{24m}.
403	\]
404	
405	The resulting class counts are
406	\[
407	\begin{array}{r|r}
408	p&k(G)\\ \hline
409	631&517\\
410	991&812\\
411	1063&871\\
412	1279&1048\\
413	1423&1166\\
414	2143&1756\\
415	2287&1874\\
416	2503&2051\\
417	2719&2228
418	\end{array}
419	\]
420	and each is strictly less than \(T(p)\).
421	
422	Here is the verification code. Besides doing the finite searches, it constructs \(O\) and \(H\) as actual matrix groups over each prime field, enumerates their elements, counts \(H\)'s conjugacy classes by conjugation orbits, verifies solvability through the normal subgroup of order eight, and tests fixed-point-freeness element by element. Thus the affine class count is certified without enumerating the much larger affine group.
423
